title: Black Wednesday: The Day One Man Beat the Bank of England

beats.say: On Wednesday the sixteenth of September, nineteen ninety two, Britain's government fought a battle against the financial markets. It raised interest rates twice in a single day. It spent billions. And it lost.

vis.text: One day. Two rate rises. A total defeat.

beats.say: The Treasury later estimated the day cost Britain around three point three billion pounds. And one investor, George Soros, reportedly made around a billion dollars betting against the pound.
He became known as the man who broke the Bank of England. So what actually happened?

vis.text: The man who broke the Bank of England.

beats.say: Part one. The ERM.

In nineteen ninety, Britain joined something called the Exchange Rate Mechanism, or ERM. It was a system that tied European currencies together, to keep exchange rates stable, as a step towards a single currency.
Britain promised to keep the pound within a narrow range against the German mark. If the pound got too weak, Britain had to defend it, by buying pounds or raising interest rates.

left.title: The promise
lines: Keep the pound in a band

beats.say: The idea was that tying the pound to Germany's strong currency would bring low inflation. But it also meant Britain couldn't freely set its own interest rates.

vis.text: Stability, at the cost of control.

beats.say: Many economists believed the pound had joined at too high a rate. That made British exports expensive and put extra strain on the economy from the start.

vis.text: Many thought the pound joined too high.

beats.say: Part two. The problem.

Then came a clash. After German reunification, Germany kept interest rates high to control inflation. Britain was in a recession, and needed lower rates. But to keep the pound in its band, it had to keep rates high too.
Traders started to believe Britain couldn't keep this up. The pound looked overvalued. Sooner or later, they thought, it would have to fall.
In the summer of nineteen ninety two, other European currencies came under pressure too, including the Italian lira. Every day, more traders joined the bet that the system would crack.

vis.title: Pressure building
items: The pound near the bottom of its band

beats.say: Part three. The bet.
George Soros's Quantum Fund built a huge bet against the pound. The idea is called shorting. You borrow pounds, sell them, and if the pound falls, you buy them back cheaper and pocket the difference.

vis.title: Shorting the pound
nodes: Buy back cheaper, keep the profit

beats.say: And the bet was lopsided. If the pound stayed in its band, he'd lose a little. If it crashed out, he'd make a fortune. Other traders were betting the same way.
Soros wasn't alone. Banks, hedge funds and companies all sold pounds. But his bet, reported at around ten billion dollars, became the most famous.

vis.text: Everyone was selling. Soros sold the most.

beats.say: Part four. Black Wednesday.
On the morning of the sixteenth of September, the selling became a flood. The Bank of England bought billions of pounds to support the price. It wasn't enough.
The government had promised it would do whatever it took to defend the pound. But every pound the Bank bought was met by more traders selling.

vis.text: Every pound bought was met with more selling.

beats.say: So the government raised interest rates, from ten percent to twelve percent. Still the selling went on. Then it announced a further rise, to fifteen percent. Still the pound fell.
Think about that. Fifteen percent interest rates in a recession would have been crushing for homeowners and businesses. And the markets simply didn't believe Britain would go through with it.
That evening, the Chancellor, Norman Lamont, announced that Britain was suspending its membership of the ERM. Interest rates went back to twelve percent, and soon fell further.

vis.text: Britain crashes out of the ERM
vis.date: Chancellor suspends membership after day of turmoil

beats.say: Next to him in the famous photographs was a young adviser named David Cameron, who would later become prime minister.

vis.text: A future prime minister stood beside him.

beats.say: Part five. The aftermath.
The pound fell sharply. Soros reportedly made more than a billion dollars. The government had spent billions defending a rate it couldn't hold.
Politically, it was a disaster for the Conservative government. Its reputation for managing the economy was badly damaged, and that damage lasted for years.
But here's the twist. Freed from the ERM, Britain could cut interest rates. The economy began to recover. Some people even started calling it White Wednesday.

After leaving the ERM, Britain adopted inflation targeting, and later made the Bank of England independent to set interest rates. Inflation stayed fairly low and the economy grew for years afterwards.
Part six. The lessons.
Black Wednesday shows that even a central bank has limits. If markets believe a currency is overvalued, and they have enough money, they can overwhelm a government's defences.

vis.title: Lessons from Black Wednesday
items: A defeat can lead to recovery

beats.say: And it played a part in Britain's later decision not to join the euro. One very expensive Wednesday helped shape Britain's relationship with Europe for decades.

vis.text: One Wednesday shaped decades of history.
